body.text: in brief
• Three Mexican men have been found guilty in the deaths of Australian surfers in Mexico.
• A judge has ruled the three Australians were murdered during a robbery gone wrong in 2024.

The parents of murdered Australian surfers Jake and Callum Robinson have said they hope three Mexican men convicted over their sons' deaths receive "significant penalties", describing the guilty verdicts as an important step towards justice.

The three Mexican nationals have been found guilty of the murders of the Australian Robinson brothers and their American friend, Jack 'Carter' Rhoad, who were killed while on a surfing holiday in Mexico in 2024.

Jesus Gerardo Garcia, known as "El Kekas," and co-defendants Irineo Francisco "N" and Angel Jesus "N" were found guilty of aggravated homicide, violent robbery and vehicle theft by a court in Baja California.
A judge ruled the three men acted with premeditation when they shot dead the men near the coastal city of Ensenada on 27 April 2024.
The defendants have yet to be sentenced.
Martin and Debra Robinson, parents of the murdered surfers, travelled from Perth to attend the four-week trial and were in court when the verdicts were handed down.

"While no verdict can ever bring back our boys or ease the heartbreak of losing them, we hope this outcome represents an important step towards justice and accountability," Debra Robinson said outside court.
"Callum and Jake had their whole lives ahead of them, filled with dreams, love and promise. We will forever carry their memory in our hearts."
The couple said they hoped the men would receive substantial prison terms when they are sentenced.
"There are significant penalties facing these people and we just hope that they get those penalties," Martin said.
What happened to the Robinson brothers?

Brothers Callum, 33, and Jake, 30, were camping and surfing near the isolated break of Punta San Jose, about 80 km south of the city of Ensenada, with their friend Rhoad, 30, when they were reported missing in late April 2024.
After a days-long search, aided by the FBI, their bodies were found on 3 May at the bottom of a well.
The victims had each suffered gunshot wounds to the head, authorities said.
Prosecutors said the accused had attempted to carjack the tourists and shot them when they resisted.
Their truck was later found burned nearby.
A witness told the court that the victims pleaded and cried for mercy in their final moments, but those pleas were met with laughter.
Handing down the verdict, the judge said he was ashamed that it happened in his country.
Parents hope for lengthy sentences
Prosecutors have requested 210 years' imprisonment for each defendant, although the maximum sentence in the state of Baja California is 60 years.
Debra said she hoped the outcome would bring some measure of peace to other families affected by defendants in Mexico.
"Hopefully they will be sentenced for a long sentence, so that they will never do this to any other Mexican family," she said.

The trial had heard evidence that the primary shooter, Gerardo, worked as a hit man for local cartel networks. He had an extensive criminal record prior to the attack and was well known to local authorities.
Asked about their feelings towards their sons' killers, the parents said they did not have "any feelings towards them".
"I have tried to hold on to the memory of my children, my sons, and I try not to think about them," Debra said.
"I don't want them to have any notoriety. We don't speak their names — they're not part of our grief."
Debra burst into tears when the guilty verdict was delivered.
Rhoad's fiancée, Natalie Weirtz, spoke via video call from the United States.
A charity in their memory
Speaking outside court, the Robinsons said attending the four-week trial was a way to honour their sons and seek justice on their behalf.
"It meant a lot to us coming here to represent our sons," Debra said through tears.
"This is the last thing that we can do for them. And it was an important part of this whole process."
The couple also announced they had established the Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation.
"We're trying to carry on the legacy of Callum and Jake," they said.
They also thanked the prosecution team, the Australian Embassy in Mexico, and the Australian Federal Police for their support throughout the case.
The girlfriend of the main defendant was sentenced in November to 20 years in prison after admitting she instigated the robbery in an attempt to steal the Australian men's truck tyres.
The woman, who was 23 at the time, was arrested days after the victims' bodies were found.
While the Ensenada area is considered relatively safe, Baja California ranks among Mexico's most violent states.
Smart Traveller advises travellers to "exercise a high degree of caution".
— With additional reporting from the Agence France-Presse and Reuters news agency.
